::: {.callout-important}
## Why learn this when TMUA is multiple choice?

You never write a proof on TMUA — every question is **multiple choice**. But almost every Paper 2 question
hides an *"if / only if / if and only if"*, and the marks turn on reading it as the right **arrow**. Get
"$A$ only if $B$" pointing the correct way in your head and half the reasoning questions fall open.
:::

<div class="fs-sub">Four ways to say a conditional — "if A then B", "A if B", "A only if B", "A if and only if B". Turn each into an arrow. The one that catches everyone: <strong>"A only if B" means A ⇒ B, not B ⇒ A.</strong></div>

## The four forms

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### "if $A$ then $B$"

$$\text{"if } A \text{ then } B\text{"}\ \equiv\ A\Rightarrow B$$
$A$ is the hypothesis, $B$ the conclusion — whenever $A$ holds, $B$ must.

[if it is raining, the ground is wet]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### "$A$ if $B$"

$$\text{"}A \text{ if } B\text{"}\ \equiv\ B\Rightarrow A$$
The **"if" clause is the hypothesis** — rearrange to "if $B$ then $A$".

[the alarm sounds if the door opens $=$ door opens $\Rightarrow$ alarm]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### "$A$ only if $B$" — the tricky one

$$\text{"}A \text{ only if } B\text{"}\ \equiv\ A\Rightarrow B$$
"Only if" points the arrow **forward**: $A$ can hold **only when** $B$ does, so $B$ is **required**.

[the bells ring only if it is Sunday $=$ bells $\Rightarrow$ Sunday (**not** Sunday $\Rightarrow$ bells)]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### "$A$ if and only if $B$"

$$\text{"}A \text{ iff } B\text{"}\ \equiv\ A\Leftrightarrow B$$
**Both** directions at once: $A\Rightarrow B$ **and** $B\Rightarrow A$.

[a triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are $60^\circ$]{.eg}
:::

::::

## Reading them, and the trap

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Turn each into an arrow

| Form | Arrow |
|---|---|
| if $A$ then $B$ | $A\Rightarrow B$ |
| $A$ if $B$ | $B\Rightarrow A$ |
| $A$ **only if** $B$ | $A\Rightarrow B$ |
| $A$ iff $B$ | $A\Leftrightarrow B$ |
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The trap — "only if"

"$A$ **only if** $B$" is $A\Rightarrow B$, **not** $B\Rightarrow A$. It reverses most people's instinct:
"only if" makes $B$ **necessary** for $A$ (without $B$, no $A$).
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Link to necessary / sufficient (cross-exam)

"$A$ **if** $B$" $=$ $B$ is **sufficient** for $A$; "$A$ **only if** $B$" $=$ $B$ is **necessary** for
$A$; "iff" $=$ both. This is Arg1, and the same wording runs through **MAT** and **STEP** reasoning.
:::

::::

## True or false? — test yourself

Two kinds of question: *is this translation into an arrow correct?* and *is this concrete statement
true?* Memorise the verdict; **the *False* ones are the traps.**

**A. Reading the forms as arrows**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| "if $A$ then $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$. | |
| "$A$ if $B$" means $B\Rightarrow A$. | |
| "$A$ only if $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$. | |
| "$A$ if and only if $B$" means both $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A$. | |
| "$A$ only if $B$" means $B\Rightarrow A$. | |
| "$A$ if $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$. | |

**B. Concrete statements**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| "A number is divisible by $4$ **only if** it is even" is true. | |
| "$x>0$ **if** $x>3$" is true. | |
| "A triangle is equilateral **if and only if** all its angles are $60^\circ$" is true. | |
| "A number is even **only if** it is divisible by $4$" is true. | |
| "$n$ is prime **if and only if** $n$ is odd" is true. | |

## Proofs of the "true or false?" facts

Decide each verdict above first, then open the key.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## A. Reading the forms as arrows — answers & proofs
- "if $A$ then $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$ — **True**: the standard reading.
- "$A$ if $B$" means $B\Rightarrow A$ — **True**: "$A$ if $B$" says $B$ is enough for $A$.
- "$A$ only if $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$ — **True**: $A$ can hold *only when* $B$ does.
- "$A$ if and only if $B$" means both $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A$ — **True**: the definition of iff.
- "$A$ only if $B$" means $B\Rightarrow A$ — **False**: it means $A\Rightarrow B$, not the reverse.
- "$A$ if $B$" means $A\Rightarrow B$ — **False**: it means $B\Rightarrow A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## B. Concrete statements — answers & proofs
- "divisible by $4$ **only if** even" is true — **True**: divisible by $4\Rightarrow$ even.
- "$x>0$ **if** $x>3$" is true — **True**: $x>3\Rightarrow x>0$.
- "equilateral **iff** all angles $60^\circ$" is true — **True**: each condition forces the other.
- "even **only if** divisible by $4$" is true — **False**: that claims even $\Rightarrow$ divisible by $4$, but $6$ is even and not divisible by $4$.
- "$n$ prime **iff** $n$ odd" is true — **False**: fails **both** ways — $2$ is prime but not odd, and $9$ is odd but not prime.
:::

## Notes

### "if $A$ then $B$" and "$A$ if $B$"

"**if $A$ then $B$**" is the plain conditional $A\Rightarrow B$: $A$ is the hypothesis, $B$ the conclusion.
"**$A$ if $B$**" says the same kind of thing but with the parts reordered — **the "if" always introduces
the hypothesis**, so "$A$ if $B$" means "if $B$ then $A$", i.e. $B\Rightarrow A$.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Write "$x>0$ if $x>3$" as an implication, and say whether it is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
The "if" introduces the hypothesis $x>3$, so it means "if $x>3$ then $x>0$", i.e. $x>3\Rightarrow x>0$.
This is **true**. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### "$A$ only if $B$" — the one everyone gets backwards

"**$A$ only if $B$**" means $A\Rightarrow B$. The phrase says $A$ can be true **only when** $B$ is true —
so $B$ is **necessary** for $A$, and the arrow runs $A\Rightarrow B$. It does **not** mean $B\Rightarrow A$.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} A town's bells ring **only if** it is Sunday. On Tuesday, are the bells ringing? On
Sunday, must they be?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
"Bells ring only if Sunday" means bells $\Rightarrow$ Sunday. **Tuesday:** since it is not Sunday, the
bells cannot be ringing (contrapositive: not Sunday $\Rightarrow$ not ringing). **Sunday:** the statement
says nothing — bells *may* ring, but need not. So "only if" gives $A\Rightarrow B$, never $B\Rightarrow A$.
$\;\blacksquare$

*If it really were "the bells ring **if** it is Sunday", that would be the other arrow, Sunday
$\Rightarrow$ bells — a different claim.*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Two ways to remember it.**
(1) **The arrowhead points at whatever follows "only if".** In "$A$ **only if** $B$", $B$ is the
destination, so $A\Rightarrow B$. (In "$A$ **if** $B$", the *if*-clause $B$ is the start, so $B\Rightarrow
A$.)
(2) **As a picture:** "$A$ only if $B$" means **$A$ sits inside $B$** — being in $A$ forces you into $B$.
:::

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "\"A only if B\" as sets: A sits inside B (A ⊆ B). Being in A forces you into B — that is A ⇒ B."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,200)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.4,3.0))
ax.plot(2.4+2.4*np.cos(t),2.4*np.sin(t),color='#1f77b4',lw=2)   # B
ax.plot(1.7+1.1*np.cos(t),1.1*np.sin(t),color='#d62728',lw=2)   # A inside B
ax.text(1.5,0,'A',fontsize=13,color='#d62728',ha='center',va='center',fontweight='bold')
ax.text(3.9,1.6,'B',fontsize=13,color='#1f77b4',ha='center',va='center',fontweight='bold')
ax.text(2.4,-3.05,'"A only if B":  A ⊆ B,  so  A ⇒ B',ha='center',fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(-0.4,5.2); ax.set_ylim(-3.4,2.8); ax.axis('off'); ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## For deeper understanding — the truth table (you never need this on the exam)

TMUA never asks you to fill a truth table or use symbols. But if you want a full check: "if $A$ then $B$"
is **false in exactly one case** — $A$ true and $B$ false — and **true otherwise**.

| $A$ | $B$ | if $A$ then $B$ | (not $A$) or $B$ | if not $B$ then not $A$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | **F** | **F** | **F** |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T |

The last three columns are **identical**, so
$$\text{"if }A\text{ then }B\text{"}\ \equiv\ \text{"(not }A\text{) or }B\text{"}\ \equiv\ \text{"if not }B\text{ then not }A\text{"}.$$
The third is the **contrapositive** (always equivalent — see S2); a handy way to rewrite "if $A$ then $B$"
is *"not $A$, or $B$"*. The **converse** "if $B$ then $A$" would give a **different** column, which is
exactly why it is not equivalent.
:::

### "$A$ if and only if $B$"

"**$A$ if and only if $B$**" combines both: the "**if**" gives $B\Rightarrow A$ and the "**only if**" gives
$A\Rightarrow B$, so together $A\Leftrightarrow B$ — $A$ and $B$ are two names for the same thing. To prove
an iff you must prove **both** directions.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is "$n$ is prime if and only if $n$ is odd" true?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**False** — and it fails in both directions. "Prime $\Rightarrow$ odd" is false ($2$ is prime and even);
"odd $\Rightarrow$ prime" is false ($9$ is odd and not prime). A single failing direction already breaks an
iff. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Link to necessary and sufficient

The forms are just necessary/sufficient in words: "$A$ **if** $B$" makes $B$ **sufficient** for $A$
($B\Rightarrow A$); "$A$ **only if** $B$" makes $B$ **necessary** for $A$ ($A\Rightarrow B$); and "iff"
makes $B$ both. Reading the arrow first, then translating to necessary/sufficient, keeps the two topics
lined up.
